turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had been patient with Sandip's oppression of his tenantry for far too long and that he would not tolerate it any longer.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip laughed and asked Nikhil if he was going to send a deputation to him, or if he would personally come to explain why his tenantry was so unhappy with Sandip's rule.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that the fate of his tenantry was of no concern to Sandip, and that he should focus on protecting his own estate from the impending attack.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip laughed loudly and asked Nikhil if he was planning to put on a show of bravery with his deputation, or if he would rather send a few lines of poetry to the Mussulmans to calm them down.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil said that he would not be mocked by Sandip's insolence and that he would take any necessary measures to protect his tenantry, even if it meant involving the authorities.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala turned to Nikhil and asked, 'What are the circumstances that have led to this impending attack, sir?'

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Bimala that the Mahomedan preachers had been spreading false propaganda and inciting the local Mussulmans against the Hindu population, and that he had reason to believe a violent confrontation was imminent.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala turned to Sandip and asked if the safety of his estate could not be linked to the well-being of the surrounding villages.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had finally found a way to scare the villagers into paying him rent with his tales of impending doom.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil insisted that the safety of the estate was inextricably linked to the security of the surrounding villages, and that any attack on the Hindus would put the entire community at risk.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that he was wasting his breath with such melodramatic warnings, and that the villagers were not about to rise up against him over some trivial matter.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip told Nikhil that his warnings sounded like the overwrought language of a bad poem, and that he was starting to think Nikhil was in the running for the title of Most Melodramatic Man in Bengal.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil told Sandip that his flippant attitude towards the situation would be his downfall, and that one day he would be forced to reap the consequences of his own actions.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Bimala, with a mischievous glint in his eye, if she had any idea why Nikhil was making such a fuss over nothing.

turns.speaker: Bimala
turns.text: Bimala asked Nikhil, with a curious expression, whether he believed that the troubles in the villages were truly as serious as he claimed they were.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip said to Nikhil that he was such a master of the dramatic, one would think he was preparing a script for a play, not warning a zamindar about real-life troubles.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: Nikhil sternly asked Sandip to stop making light of the situation, warning him that the consequences of such carelessness would be dire.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip said to Nikhil that one would think the local Mussulmans were about to invade Bengal, judging by the way Nikhil was carrying on.

turns.speaker: Nikhil
turns.text: The situation was grave and the zamindar's flippant attitude only served to exacerbate the dangers they all faced.

turns.speaker: Sandip
turns.text: Sandip asked Nikhil, with a smirk, if the local Mussulmans were planning to take over the zamindari, and if so, where he intended to hide his precious books.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Bimala where she would go, addressing her as the Queen.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he kept Browning among his books, reminding him of a contest they had over translating lines from Browning, and inquiring if Nikhil remembered it.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil and Bimala that he had managed to translate the lines into Bengali, but the result was unlikely to be well-received, and that he had once thought he was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence had intervened to prevent it, and he recalled old Dakshina's poetry.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Bimala that it was pointless to search the bookshelves, as Nikhil no longer read poetry since his marriage, but that he, Sandip, was about to be afflicted with the 'fever fit of poesy' again.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil warned Sandip that he had come to give him a warning.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was warning him about the 'fever fit of poesy'.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that for some time, Mahomedan preachers had been stirring up the local Mussulmans, who were angry with Sandip and might attack him at any moment.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he had come to advise him to flee.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had come to give him information, not advice.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip told Nikhil that if the estates were his, a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for him, and that Nikhil should intimidate the preachers instead of frightening him, and that Nikhil's weakness was also affecting his neighbouring zamindars.

opening.speaker: Nikhil
opening.text: Nikhil told Sandip that he had not offered him advice, and that he wished Sandip would refrain from giving him his advice, as it was useless, and that there was another thing he wanted to tell Sandip, namely that Sandip and his followers had been secretly oppressing Nikhil's tenantry, and that he could no longer allow that, so he must ask Sandip to leave his territory.

opening.speaker: Sandip
opening.text: Sandip asked Nikhil if he was threatening him with fear of the Mussulmans, or if there was another fear he had to threaten him with.
